Bidisha: yes. passed
Nazia: BIDISHA!!! 🎉 I'm screaming

Nazia: oh. sorry, I got carried away
Bidisha: no it's okay, you're sweet. I think I'm just relieved and flat

Bidisha: thank you. that means a lot 🙂
Nazia: want to just get chai tomorrow and not talk about it?

Nazia: I'll bring the good biscuits
Bidisha: and no questions about my marks
Nazia: promise. only tea and gossip

qa.a: Nazia suggested getting chai tomorrow.

qa.a: Give a brief specific note of pride and offer a quiet plan like chai, as Nazia did.

qa.a: Nazia likely felt a bit sheepish, saying sorry for getting carried away, and then switched to quieter support like chai tomorrow.

passage: When the board results were read out at the village school in Bihar, Arnab's name was at the top of the list. He stood at the back of the crowd, wide-eyed but silent. Gopika, his friend since childhood, felt like leaping and shouting. She nearly did. But she noticed his hands trembling and how he kept looking at the ground. She walked over, put her hand lightly on his arm and said, "I saw the hours you put in. I'm really proud of you." Arnab let out a long breath, and his eyes filled. "Thank you," he said. Gopika left the loud celebration to the others for now, and stayed beside him.

qa.q: Where was Arnab's name on the list?
qa.a: Arnab's name was at the top of the list.

qa.q: What was Arnab feeling at the back of the crowd?
qa.a: Arnab was overwhelmed and probably relieved, shown by the wide eyes, silence, trembling hands and filling eyes. He might also have felt the pressure of the result, so joy was not the only feeling.

qa.q: What did Gopika do that fit Arnab's mood?
qa.a: She held back her shouting and gave a short, specific note of pride, staying beside Arnab.

qa.q: How might the loud celebrating crowd have looked to Arnab?
qa.a: It may have felt too much for Arnab right then, so Gopika's quiet way suited him better.

grounding: A young adult congratulates a friend on an exam result, matching enthusiasm to the friend's mood with a brief specific note of pride.

passage: Beatriz got the job offer from the Berlin architecture firm on a Tuesday. Freya heard the news from a friend, grabbed a bottle of sparkling juice and a party hat, and ran to Beatriz's flat in Lisbon, ready to scream. But when Beatriz opened the door, her eyes were red. Her grandmother had been in hospital all week, and moving meant leaving her. Freya quietly put the party hat back in her bag. "I heard. Congratulations. Are you okay?" Beatriz shrugged. "I don't know if I'm happy." They sat on the step. After a while Freya said, "For what it's worth, you worked for three years on that portfolio. I watched you redo the museum drawing seven times. I'm proud of you." Beatriz smiled for the first time. "Seven times. You counted?" "Someone had to." They drank the juice, quietly, without the hat.

qa.q: How many times did Beatriz redo the museum drawing?
qa.a: Seven times.

qa.q: What was Beatriz feeling about the job offer?
qa.a: She was torn, unsure if she was happy, because taking the job meant leaving her grandmother, who had been in hospital all week.

qa.q: What did Freya do that made her congratulations feel sincere?
qa.a: She put away the party hat, matched Beatriz's quiet mood, and gave a brief, specific note of pride about the portfolio.

qa.q: What would change if Freya had burst in cheering?
qa.a: It might have felt performative and out of tune with Beatriz's worry, making it harder for her to share her mixed feelings.

grounding: Shows a young adult matching congratulations to a friend's mixed mood with a brief, specific note of pride.

passage: On result day, the whole hostel crowded round the notice board. Deepika found her own name, top ten, and then Gargi's, just above the pass line. Deepika wanted to shriek "You passed! Party tonight!" But she remembered Gargi had failed two subjects last semester and had been studying till three every night. Gargi stood very still, reading the list twice. Other girls were hugging and screaming around them. Deepika touched Gargi's arm gently. "You did it." Gargi's eyes filled. "Barely." "You cleared both subjects you failed last time. I saw you studying at three every night. That's not barely." Gargi laughed, a little wet. "Can we just get chai? No party." "Chai," Deepika said. Later, on the hostel group, someone posted "Gargi PASSED 🎉🥳". Gargi muted it, and messaged Deepika: "Thank you for the chai version."

qa.q: What did Gargi ask to do instead of a party?
qa.a: Just get chai.

qa.q: What was Gargi feeling as she read the list twice?
qa.a: She was relieved but also embarrassed and fragile, seeing her name just above the pass line; her eyes filled when Deepika spoke.

qa.q: Why did Deepika's quiet congratulations work better than a loud one?
qa.a: It matched Gargi's mood and named a specific effort, so it felt sincere instead of performative.

qa.q: What would change if Deepika had shrieked "Party tonight!" at the notice board?
qa.a: Gargi might have felt exposed and pushed into a celebration she didn't feel, much like the loud group post she later muted.

grounding: Shows a young adult matching congratulations to a friend's mood with specific, sincere words instead of overdone cheer.

passage:
Dear Jasleen,
I heard from Harpreet that you got the job at the children's hospital in Amritsar. I wanted to write properly instead of sending a string of emojis.
I remember the night in second year when you came back from your hospital placement and couldn't eat because a little boy had cried all through his injection and you'd held his hand the whole time. You said then, "That's where I want to be." And now you will be.
I know you've been tired and worried about the move and leaving your mother alone, so I'm not going to shout. I just want you to know I'm proud of you. Truly.
When you're settled, I'll come visit and you can show me the ward.
Tenzin

qa.q: Where is Jasleen's new job?
qa.a: At the children's hospital in Amritsar.

qa.q: What might Jasleen be feeling about the new job?
qa.a: Jasleen is probably proud and happy, but also tired and worried about moving and leaving a mother alone.

qa.q: What makes Tenzin's congratulations feel sincere?
qa.a: It is brief and specific, recalling the night Jasleen held a crying boy's hand, and it respects Jasleen's tired, worried mood instead of shouting.

qa.q: What would change if Tenzin had sent only a string of emojis?
qa.a: It might have felt quick and performative, missing Jasleen's mixed feelings and the personal memory that shows real pride.

grounding: Shows a young adult congratulating a friend with a brief, specific note of pride that matches the friend's mood.

passage: So, you asked on the podcast about the best congratulations I ever gave. I'm Madhuri, and honestly I learnt it by getting it wrong first. When my flatmate Jahnavi got her job offer from the Chennai firm, I burst into her room with a party popper and a speaker blasting dance music. She smiled, but it was a thin smile. She said thanks and went back to her laptop. Later I saw her on the balcony, very quiet. The job meant leaving her mother alone in Nagpur, and she was proud and sad at the same time. My confetti had drowned all of that. The next morning I left a note on her chai mug: "You earned this with every late night I watched you work. I'm proud of you, and I'm here for the hard parts too." She came to find me with the note in her hand and hugged me for a long time. That was the real congratulations.

qa.q: Where was Jahnavi's job offer from?
qa.a: The Chennai firm.

qa.q: What did Madhuri feel on seeing Jahnavi quiet on the balcony?
qa.a: Madhuri felt a pang of regret, sensing that the loud celebration had drowned out Jahnavi's mixed feelings.

qa.q: What made the note work better than the party popper?
qa.a: It was brief, specific about Jahnavi's effort and made room for both pride and sadness, matching her mood instead of performing cheer.

qa.q: What was the party popper moment like for Jahnavi?
qa.a: Proud but sad about leaving her mother, Jahnavi probably felt the loud cheer didn't fit her mood, so she gave a thin smile and withdrew.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult learning to match congratulations to a friend's mood, where a brief, specific note of pride feels more sincere than overdone cheer.
